title: Overall, the questions follow the same path and highlight experiences and opinions of shopping online. As for how I would conduct an analysis, I would start by reading all the data through one full time without making any notes as an initial familiarization with the data.  Once I have read them all once, I would organize the data into individual responses to each question so that I can try to understand each individual's unique perspective.  Once I have read the interviews in these different ways, I would read again but start making labels of the specific sections.  An example would be taking words like easy, simple, or convenient and labeling them all as ease of use, keeping a log of each time ease of use is mentioned.  I would do this with all sections and try to assign labels to each response, to start building out a list of common themes without trying to force phrases into specific categories they do not belong in.  Once I built out the first set of labels, or codes, I would go through and organize these common codes into second-order labels which organizes the data in a much easier to digest manner.  I would then continue to follow the six-phase process of thematic analysis, eventually generating discussion around potential findings. I would do my best to leave out my personal opinions on responses as this is not relevant but would take note if any labels seem to align with research questions or specific phenomena.  As for my personal reactions to the data sets, it appears similar to how I responded personally and to how I responded as the target demographic.

title: he content also reminded me that participants can discuss the same experience without assigning it the same meaning. Several comments appeared to gain clarity as participants responded to one another, whereas other reactions remained individual or conditional. Consequently, I would need to consider not only what was said, but also how each response developed within the group conversation. My strongest reaction was an increased appreciation for the restraint qualitative analysis requires. The task is not to select the most compelling statements, but to develop an interpretation that remains faithful to the range and context of the participants’ accounts.

title: My first thought on the sample data was that there was a lot to wade through, but I could also see some common ideas emerging. In each of the focus groups, they talked about many of the same things, such as convenience, sizing, returns, website problems and not always knowing how an item will actually look or feel when they receive it. If I was looking at this data I would begin by reading each transcript a couple of times before coding anything. I think that would help me get a better sense of what the participants are actually saying before I start to decide what the themes are. Amankwaa (2016) discusses the importance of trustworthiness in qualitative research so I would also ensure that I document my development of my codes and themes and keep the participants’ responses at the core of my analysis.

title:
I found the sample focus group data to be rich, detailed, and highly insightful, offering a deep understanding of consumers’ online fashion browsing and shopping behaviors. Participants openly shared their motivations, frustrations, preferences, and actions, which immediately caught my attention. As I reviewed the data, several common themes emerged, including convenience, product visualization, sizing issues, delivery concerns, and the need to evaluate product quality before buying. If I were conducting the analysis, I would need to read the transcripts several times before making decisions about themes. I would first identify recurring experiences and develop meaning units that remain close to what participants actually described. From there, I would compare those meaning units across the focus groups and look for confirming evidence as well as comments that challenge my initial interpretation. This feels particularly important because some experiences are connected but do not necessarily mean the same thing. For example, participants consistently valued the convenience of online shopping, yet that convenience was complicated by uncertainty about sizing, fit, fabric, and whether the product received would match what was presented online.

The visualization discussion was the part of the data I found most interesting. Participants generally responded positively to features that allowed them to see fabric texture, garment movement, different angles, and other product details. At the same time, their responses suggested that simply adding more technology does not necessarily make the shopping experience better. Some questioned whether particular features provided enough useful information, while others wanted clothing displayed on models with different sizes and body shapes. My initial interpretation is that the underlying issue may be less about visualization itself and more about reducing uncertainty. Overall, working through the sample data helped me better understand why qualitative analysis requires patience and restraint. The challenge is not finding interesting statements. It is determining which patterns are sufficiently supported across the data to justify moving from individual experiences to broader meaning units and themes. Comments often shifted among browsing habits, prior purchases, website features, and reactions to visualization technology. I would begin by reading each transcript independently and writing brief notes about my immediate reactions, questions, and possible assumptions. Keeping those reflections separate from the participant data would help me recognize where my interpretation might be influenced by personal expectations. I would then reread the transcripts to examine recurring language and experiences, while remaining attentive to comments that differ from the general direction of each discussion. Only after completing that process would I compare the three focus groups and begin making decisions about how the data should be organized.

The content also reminded me that participants can discuss the same experience without assigning it the same meaning. Several comments appeared to gain clarity as participants responded to one another, whereas other reactions remained individual or conditional.

Data Collection Steps and Analysis While planning the data collection procedures for my proposed study, “To what extent does leadership trust predict employee knowledge-sharing behavior among middle managers in U.S. workplace organizations?”, I am focusing on maintaining alignment among the research question, variables, instruments, sampling strategy, recruitment procedures, and planned statistical analysis. Because this study uses a quantitative correlational predictive design, each data-collection step must produce the type of numerical data needed to test the relationship between leadership trust and employee knowledge-sharing behavior.

Proposed Data & Collection Steps

My proposed data-collection process will occur in the following sequence:

    Obtain the necessary approval before recruitment.
    I will complete the required Capella University Institutional Review Board (IRB) process before collecting data. The recruitment materials, informed-consent language, eligibility criteria, survey instruments, and data-collection procedures will be finalized as part of this process.
    Finalize the survey instrument.
    The survey will be administered through Qualtrics. The instrument will include informed consent, screening questions, demographic questions needed to describe the sample, the leadership trust measure, and the knowledge-sharing behavior measure. I plan to use the McAllister (1995) trust measure for leadership trust and the Van den Hooff and de Ridder (2004) knowledge-sharing measure for knowledge-sharing behavior.
    Conduct a power analysis.
    Before recruitment, I will use an a priori power analysis to determine the minimum sample size necessary for the planned simple linear regression. My current target is approximately 150–250 participants, but the final minimum will be supported by the power analysis rather than selected arbitrarily.
    Establish participant eligibility.
    Participants will be adults who work in U.S.-based workplace organizations and currently hold a middle-management or supervisory position. Participants will also need sufficient experience with their current supervisor to meaningfully evaluate leadership trust. My proposed eligibility requirement is at least six months working under the current supervisor.
    Recruit participants.
    I plan to use purposive and snowball sampling. Recruitment may occur through professional organizations, LinkedIn, relevant professional networks, and other appropriate organizational or professional channels. Recruitment materials will explain the study, eligibility requirements, voluntary nature of participation, confidentiality, and survey access.
    Administer the anonymous survey.
    Eligible participants will access the Qualtrics survey, review informed consent, complete the screening questions, and then complete the research measures. I will avoid collecting unnecessary identifying information.
    Monitor data collection.
    I will monitor response rates and eligibility while avoiding changes to the procedures that could introduce bias. I will determine whether additional recruitment is necessary based on the power analysis and the number of usable responses obtained.
    Prepare the dataset for analysis.
    After data collection closes, I will examine the dataset for incomplete responses, duplicate responses, missing data, and other data-quality concerns. I will score the instruments according to their established procedures and create composite scores for leadership trust and knowledge-sharing behavior.
    Conduct the planned statistical analysis.
    The final dataset will be analyzed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression. The regression will test whether leadership trust statistically predicts employee knowledge-sharing behavior.

Weak or Potentially Problematic Steps

The recruitment and sampling process is currently the weakest part of my plan. Purposive and snowball sampling are appropriate for reaching a specific population that may be difficult to identify through a sampling frame, but they limit generalizability. Participants who respond through professional networks or LinkedIn may differ from eligible middle managers who do not participate in those networks.

A second concern is obtaining enough participants who meet the middle-manager eligibility criteria. Simply recruiting working adults would not adequately address the research question. I therefore need to ensure that screening questions clearly establish participants' managerial responsibilities and their experience with their current supervisor.

A third concern involves common-method bias. Participants will provide self-reported perceptions of leadership trust and their own knowledge-sharing behavior in the same survey. This creates the possibility that relationships between the variables could be influenced by the method used to collect the data rather than by the constructs themselves. Anonymous participation, clear instructions, neutral wording, and established instruments should help reduce some of this concern, although they cannot eliminate it completely.

A fourth concern is the possibility of insufficient statistical power. Recruiting a convenient number of participants is not enough. I need to complete the a priori power analysis before recruitment so that the minimum sample size is justified statistically.

Finally, instrument permissions and exact scoring procedures require additional attention. Before launching the survey, I need to verify the appropriate use or permission requirements for the selected instruments and confirm that the wording, response scale, scoring, and administration procedures are consistent with the original sources.

Support Needed to Address These Concerns

The most important support I need is guidance from my instructor and Capella's IRB resources regarding recruitment procedures, informed consent, and the appropriate use of LinkedIn and professional organizations for participant recruitment. I also need to verify whether permission is required for the selected instruments and whether the instruments can be reproduced directly in Qualtrics.

I will also use G*Power or an equivalent power-analysis resource to establish the minimum sample size for simple linear regression. This will provide a stronger justification for the planned sample than simply stating that I intend to collect 150–250 responses.

Finally, reviewing the Project Plan Alignment Tracking and Alignment Map: GuidingQuestions resources is helpful because they encourage me to examine whether every proposed data-collection step contributes directly to answering the research question rather than collecting information simply because it is available.

Data Collection & Research Gap

The alignment process is particularly important for my study because the identified gap is specific. The literature does not simply lack research on leadership, trust, or knowledge sharing. Instead, the gap concerns the specific relationship between leadership trust and employee knowledge-sharing behavior among middle managers in U.S. workplace organizations.

This alignment helps prevent unnecessary data collection. For example, I do not need to collect extensive information about organizational performance, employee satisfaction, or multiple leadership styles because those variables are not necessary to answer my research question.

Thanks,


Pamela, I like how detailed your data collection plan is, especially your decision to complete the power analysis before settling on a final sample size. That is something I am also going to need to address in my own quantitative study because the number of participants should be statistically justified rather than based on an arbitrary target. Your concern about common method bias also stood out to me because both of your variables are being measured through the same self reported survey. I think recognizing that limitation now gives you an opportunity to build safeguards into the study before data collection begins. I am curious about your recruitment strategy, though. Since purposive and snowball sampling limit generalizability, have you considered whether a third party participant provider could identify qualified middle managers and allow you to use a probability based sampling approach instead?

Generic Qualitative Interviews study is a semi-structured,critical-incident interview protocol administered by the researcher The primary data-collection instrument for this Generic Qualitative Interviews study is a semi-structured, critical-incident interview protocol administered by the researcher, who is the instrument (Merriam & Tisdell, 2016; Seidman, 2019). Interviews last approximately 60–75 minutes by encrypted video conference only after informed consent and recording permission, which is the first ethical control before any infrastructure event is discussed. The protocol opens with the participant’s IT or network role and the IT disaster recovery platform-as-a-service (ITDRPaaS) or functionally equivalent external recovery platform in use, then asks for one disruption, failover, recovery test, or production recovery so that talk is anchored in a concrete infrastructure event rather than in abstract policy (Flanagan, 1954; Kvale & Brinkmann, 2015). Open-ended probes, not yes-or-no items, elicit how managers experienced who counted, who decided failover or restore, and what counted as proof that infrastructure was recoverable. Field notes captured during and immediately after each session record hesitations and reflexivity cues without scoring recovery performance or inspecting live systems. The interview guide will receive chair or methodologist expert review before Institutional Review Board submission so that wording, burden, and leading-question risk are examined before any human-subjects contact.

The protocol begins with inquiries into the participant’s IT or network role and the IT disaster recovery platform-as-a-service (ITDRPaaS) or an equivalent external recovery platform in use. Open-ended probes, rather than yes-or-no questions, elicit insights into how managers perceived accountability, decision-making regarding failover or restoration, and the criteria for determining the recoverability of infrastructure. Good Day Dr. Munchick and Class,

Discuss the methodology that you have chosen at this time. Why did you choose this for your project?

The methodological approach for this study will be a generic qualitative inquiry, selected to investigate how U.S. small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) IT/network managers perceive and interpret the governance challenges associated with establishing and managing IT Disaster Recovery Plan as a Service (ITDRPaaS). This approach is aligned with the study’s topic and problem, as the research aims to describe and interpret participant perceptions of governance practices as managers translate organizational IT strategy into operational disaster recovery actions. Generic qualitative inquiry is particularly suitable for this study because it focuses on understanding how individuals make sense of processes, decisions, and organizational conditions without requiring strict philosophical assumptions associated with phenomenology or other qualitative traditions (Creswell & Poth, 2016).

The general problem is that many U.S. small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) suffer avoidable organizational harm during cyber disruptions because they fail to consistently translate IT Disaster Recovery as a Service (ITDRPaaS) capabilities into governed, auditable, and defensible recover-ability assurance. This inconsistency is particularly pronounced when decision authority is fragmented and oversight is applied inconsistently under pressure (Lowry et al., 2025).

My view on IT and network managers within U.S. SMEs, who bear the responsibility for recovery while attempting to coordinate across both internal teams and external service providers in environments where stakeholder priorities are often in flux. Furthermore, existing governance frameworks frequently fail to establish clear decision rights, accountability structures, or time-sensitive escalation pathways (Erdiaw-Kwasie et al., 2017 & Mitchell et al., 1997). This responsibility of stakeholders-salience to be fascinating to see how stakeholders clamor when things go wrong withing Small and mediun IT enterprises.

search_text:
wk4 Good Evening Dr. Muchnick and Class,

The primary data source for my study will be Generic Qualitative Interviews (Changed from Lived Perspective and Initial week 2 paper), specifically semi-structured interviews, with approximately 12–15 specific selected IT Network managers/CIO/CFO from U.S. small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). These participants will have experience in implementing or overseeing IT Disaster Recovery Planning as a Service (ITDRPaaS). Purposive criterion sampling is suitable for this qualitative inquiry since it seeks information-rich participants who possess direct knowledge of the subject matter, rather than aiming for statistically representative samples (Patton, 2015). Within the Generic Qualitative Interviews framework, participants will be chosen for their ability to provide detailed insights into organizational governance processes, stakeholder interactions, decision-making authority, escalation pathways, and practices related to recoverability assurance (Merriam & Tisdell, 2016). The interviews will include a critical-incident component, allowing managers to recount specific experiences related to disruptions, fail-overs, testing, or recovery events. My interview will also explain how stakeholder pressure influenced governance actions under time constraints (Kvale & Brinkmann, 2015).

This approach directly aligns with the research purpose by enabling participants to articulate how governance decisions are understood and enacted within their organizations, rather than focusing on predetermined variables. Consequently, this primary data source will provide descriptive insights into how IT Network managers/CIO/CFO perceive stakeholder salience and its translation into decision-making authority, escalation processes, and evidence of recoverability during stakeholder ITDRPaaS-mediated recovery.

References:

Kvale, S. and Brinkmann, S. (2015) Interviews: Learning the Craft of Qualitative Research Interviewing. 3rd Edition, Sage Publications, Thousand Oaks, CA. https://doi-org.library.capella.edu/10.1002/nha3.202

Merriam, S. B., & Tisdell, E. J. (2016). Qualitative research: A guide to design and implementation (4th ed.). Jossey-Bass.

Patton, M. Q. (2015). The sociological roots of utilization-focused evaluation. The American Sociologist, 46(4), 457-462. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12108-015-9275-8

excerpt: n this study, ITDRPaaS stakeholders are defined as individuals with a vested interest in the organizational, technical, governance, risk, compliance, or service-provider aspects of how U.S. small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) prepare for, govern, execute, and validate cloud
search_text:
wk5 n this study, ITDRPaaS stakeholders are defined as individuals with a vested interest in the organizational, technical, governance, risk, compliance, or service-provider aspects of how U.S. small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) prepare for, govern, execute, and validate cloud-based disaster recovery. From a stakeholder-salience perspective, their importance lies in the varying degrees of influence they possess, characterized by power, legitimacy, and urgency. These factors can impact recovery priorities, decision-making authority, escalation timing, and the standards of evidence required for demonstrating recoverability (Mitchell et al., 1997). The participant pool is expected to can include IT network managers, infrastructure or cloud managers, cybersecurity and compliance managers, CFOs, CIOs, owners or senior executives with recovery decision authority, and representatives/providers who directly assist U.S. SMEs. Criterion-based purposive sampling is deemed suitable, as the goal is not to gather a statistically representative sample of all U.S. SME leadership grouping, but rather to identify approximately 10–15 information-rich participants capable of detailing the governance processes, recovery decisions, escalation events, provider dependencies, and evidence-acceptance practices related to ITDRPaaS (Merriam & Tisdell, 2016; Patton, 2015).

References:

Merriam, S. B., & Tisdell, E. J. (2016). Qualitative research: A guide to design and implementation (4th ed.). Jossey-Bass.

Mitchell, R. K., Agle, B. R., & Wood, D. J. (1997). Toward a theory of stakeholder identification and salience: Defining the principle of who and what really counts. Academy of Management Review, 22(4), 853–886.

title: The proposed study employs stakeholder theory as its broad theoretical foundation and stakeholder-salience theory as its middle-range operational lens. Power, legitimacy, and urgency function as sensitizing concepts for examining how organizational actors interpret and prioritize competing recovery claims. The study conceptualizes stakeholder prioritization as operating through decision-rights allocation, escalation pathways, exception authority, and evidence-acceptance practices that collectively shape recoverability assurance. Accordingly, the SAL → DR → ESC → AE relationship is positioned as a proposed, contingency-sensitive conceptual process model rather than an established theory. Through generic qualitative inquiry, critical-incident prompts, reflexive analysis, and interview–artifact triangulation, the study will examine whether empirical evidence supports, refines, extends, complicates, or contradicts the proposed governance-to-assurance mechanism.

title: The proposed study employs stakeholder theory as its broad theoretical foundation and stakeholder-salience theory as its middle-range operational lens. Power, legitimacy, and urgency function as sensitizing concepts for examining how organizational actors interpret and prioritize competing recovery claims. The study conceptualizes stakeholder prioritization as operating through decision-rights allocation, escalation pathways, exception authority, and evidence-acceptance practices that collectively shape recoverability assurance. Accordingly, the SAL → DR → ESC → AE relationship is positioned as a proposed, contingency-sensitive conceptual process model rather than an established theory. Through generic qualitative inquiry, critical-incident prompts, reflexive analysis, and interview–artifact triangulation, the study will examine whether empirical evidence supports, refines, extends, complicates, or contradicts the proposed governance-to-assurance mechanism.

excerpt: This generic qualitative inquiry will establish methodological rigor through the trustworthiness criteria of credibility, dependability, confirmability, and transferability rather than through quantitative measures such as Cronbach’s alpha, which assesses the internal consistency
search_text: This generic qualitative inquiry will establish methodological rigor through the trustworthiness criteria of credibility, dependability, confirmability, and transferability rather than through quantitative measures such as Cronbach’s alpha, which assesses the internal consistency of scale-based instruments (Lincoln & Guba, 1985). Potential threats include researcher bias when interpreting stakeholder salience through power, legitimacy, and urgency (PLU); inconsistent interview probing; participant recall and social-desirability bias; coercive recruitment conditions; inaccurate transcription; premature theme development; and insufficient corroboration of participant accounts. Credibility will be strengthened through purposive recruitment of qualified U.S. SME IT/network managers, a standardized semi-structured interview protocol with critical-incident prompts, transcript verification, negative-case analysis, and triangulation of participant accounts with available recovery plans, escalation procedures, test reports, and recoverability-assurance records. Dependability will be supported through consistent data-collection procedures and an audit trail documenting the progression from excerpts and meaning units to codes, categories, themes, and conclusions. Confirmability will be strengthened through reflexive journaling and documentation of theoretical and analytical decisions, particularly when PLU operates as a sensitizing framework. Transferability will be supported through contextual descriptions of U.S. SME conditions, ITDRPaaS arrangements, stakeholder relationships, decision rights, escalation pathways, evidence standards, and third-party dependencies, while pseudonyms, organizational masking, and data de-identification will protect confidentiality. Together, these procedures will provide a traceable and defensible basis for interpreting how stakeholder-salience dynamics shape the governance-to-assurance chain through which U.S. SMEs seek to produce and sustain recoverability assurance (Korstjens & Moser, 2018; Lincoln & Guba, 1985; Merriam & Tisdell, 2016; Nowell et al., 2017).

title: Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual
excerpt: Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students
search_text: Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students adapt to this space, and encouraging students' critical research and writing skills in this space. Although students enter our classrooms well versed in writing-related values and ideas relayed to them in their past school experiences, often this instruction does not address—or does not go far enough in addressing—issues of online research and writing. First-year composition seems, to us, to be the ideal place to initiate discussions related to such issues; first-year composition courses tackle (among many other functions) the task of acculturating students into academic writing. Because academic writing now relies so heavily on the reading, writing, and research accessed via virtual spaces, it is necessary for first-year composition courses to address research and writing in electronic realms and to help students develop techniques that will aid them to best use these systems. From this perspective, we address the intersections of online research and plagiarism, discuss how we can best handle plagiarism in our first-year classrooms, and how we can best equip students with the tools necessary to do appropriate research—both online and offline. (p. 193)

excerpt: Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students
search_text: Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students adapt to this space, and encouraging students' critical research and writing skills in this space. Although students enter our classrooms well versed in writing-related values and ideas relayed to them in their past school experiences, often this instruction does not address—or does not go far enough in addressing—issues of online research and writing. First-year composition seems, to us, to be the ideal place to initiate discussions related to such issues; first-year composition courses tackle (among many other functions) the task of acculturating students into academic writing. Because academic writing now relies so heavily on the reading, writing, and research accessed via virtual spaces, it is necessary for first-year composition courses to address research and writing in electronic realms and to help students develop techniques that will aid them to best use these systems. From this perspective, we address the intersections of online research and plagiarism, discuss how we can best handle plagiarism in our first-year classrooms, and how we can best equip students with the tools necessary to do appropriate research—both online and offline. (p. 193)

title: Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual
excerpt: Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students
search_text: Two beliefs scaffold this article: First, we are witnessing students adapting their literacy, research, reading, and writing skills and processes to the virtual space—and complexity—of the World Wide Web. Second, first-year composition teachers have a key role in helping students adapt to this space, and encouraging students' critical research and writing skills in this space. Although students enter our classrooms well versed in writing-related values and ideas relayed to them in their past school experiences, often this instruction does not address—or does not go far enough in addressing—issues of online research and writing. First-year composition seems, to us, to be the ideal place to initiate discussions related to such issues; first-year composition courses tackle (among many other functions) the task of acculturating students into academic writing. Because academic writing now relies so heavily on the reading, writing, and research accessed via virtual spaces, it is necessary for first-year composition courses to address research and writing in electronic realms and to help students develop techniques that will aid them to best use these systems. From this perspective, we address the intersections of online research and plagiarism, discuss how we can best handle plagiarism in our first-year classrooms, and how we can best equip students with the tools necessary to do appropriate research—both online and offline. (p. 193)

This paraphrase includes several word units that match the original text exactly: "writing-related values and ideas," "past school experiences," and "online research and writing." The unit "did not cover or go far enough in covering" matches the phrasing of "does not address—or does not go far enough in addressing" while merely changing the verb address to cover. Another error in this paraphrase is the use of the verb purported: Purport means to put forth as true, or to falsely claim, so writers should not use purport when they mean assert. Ineffective. This paraphrase includes three word units that match the original text exactly: "writing-related values and ideas," "past school experience," "issues of online research and writing." Also, the paraphrase misrepresents the original sentence in that it introduces the idea that the students' previous education was in some way a failure; the original sentence indicates that the previous instruction may not have gone as deeply as is now required in post-secondary education, but the original does not give any indication of failure. Effective. This paraphrase captures the key points of the original sentence, is about the same length as the original sentence, and is written in the writer's own words. excerpt: We reflect on the past, present, and future of stakeholder theory, focusing on its link to strategy and organization scholarship. Stakeholder theory was originally conceived as a theory of strategic management, but for most of its history it largely developed without having a not
search_text: We reflect on the past, present, and future of stakeholder theory, focusing on its link to strategy and organization scholarship. Stakeholder theory was originally conceived as a theory of strategic management, but for most of its history it largely developed without having a noticeable impact on strategy research. This has changed in the past decade, however, with the strategy field making a “stakeholder turn.” We highlight the streams of research at the forefront of this turn, including work on “behavioral stakeholder theory,” ‘stakeholder strategy theory,’ and “stakeholder governance.” We conclude with an outlook on how stakeholder theory can help strategy scholars develop a theory of managing value creation that explicitly acknowledges both the economic and moral nature of relationships in and around organizations.

title: Stakeholder theory was originally developed as a theory of, or perhaps rather a perspective on, strategic management (Freeman, 1984). However, subsequent work r
excerpt: Stakeholder theory was originally developed as a theory of, or perhaps rather a perspective on, strategic management (Freeman, 1984). However, subsequent work remained largely disconnected from developments in the strategy field because strategy scholars became increasingly conce
search_text: Stakeholder theory was originally developed as a theory of, or perhaps rather a perspective on, strategic management (Freeman, 1984). However, subsequent work remained largely disconnected from developments in the strategy field because strategy scholars became increasingly concerned with grounding their work in economic theories and concepts (e.g. Rumelt et al., 1991), while stakeholder theorists became increasingly concerned with grounding their theory in normative ethics (Dmytriyev et al., 2021). Over the past 10–15 years, however, the strategy field has made a “stakeholder turn,” with more and more mainstream strategy scholars adopting a stakeholder perspective (e.g. Barney, 2018; Klein et al., 2012; Zollo et al., 2018). In this essay, we reflect on this stakeholder turn, interpreting it as an attempt to develop a new type of strategy theory.

title: We do so in three steps. First, we consider how the initially diverging developmental paths of stakeholder theory and strategic management scholarship have begu
excerpt: We do so in three steps. First, we consider how the initially diverging developmental paths of stakeholder theory and strategic management scholarship have begun to reconverge. We then give an overview of the main strands of strategic management scholarship that have furthered st
search_text: We do so in three steps. First, we consider how the initially diverging developmental paths of stakeholder theory and strategic management scholarship have begun to reconverge. We then give an overview of the main strands of strategic management scholarship that have furthered stakeholder theory over the course of the past decade. Finally, we reflect on how the reconvergence of stakeholder theory and strategy theory can help strategy and organization scholars develop “clear thinking about the organization of stakeholders and their cooperative role in value creation.” In particular, we discuss how what McGahan (2021) refers to as the “new stakeholder theory” (NST) implies a promise of a new type of strategy theory: a theory of value creation and value appropriation that explicitly and simultaneously addresses the economic and moral side of human organization.

excerpt: Stakeholder theory is typically traced back to Edward Freeman’s (1984) book Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach. Although Freeman’s book was a strategic management text, stakeholder theory and strategic management subsequently developed largely in isolation from each oth
search_text: Stakeholder theory is typically traced back to Edward Freeman’s (1984) book Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach. Although Freeman’s book was a strategic management text, stakeholder theory and strategic management subsequently developed largely in isolation from each other (Bosse and Sutton, 2019; Dmytriyev et al., 2021). One reason for this is that Freeman’s book coincided with an economic turn in strategy research (Wicks and Harrison, 2017): in the 1980s, research in the newly established field of strategic management became increasingly grounded in economic theorizing (e.g. Barney, 1991; Porter, 1980; Rumelt et al., 1991).

title: Since its inception, stakeholder theory has explicitly positioned itself as an alternative to economic theorizing (Freeman et al., 2010). Whereas traditional ec
excerpt: Since its inception, stakeholder theory has explicitly positioned itself as an alternative to economic theorizing (Freeman et al., 2010). Whereas traditional economic theorizing emphasizes market competition as the main driver of social welfare, stakeholder theory emphasizes coop
search_text: Since its inception, stakeholder theory has explicitly positioned itself as an alternative to economic theorizing (Freeman et al., 2010). Whereas traditional economic theorizing emphasizes market competition as the main driver of social welfare, stakeholder theory emphasizes cooperation (Freeman and Phillips, 2002). Whereas traditional economic theorizing, and in particular agency theory, sees managers’ duty as maximizing the financial market value of firms (Friedman, 1970; Jensen, 2002), stakeholder theory holds that the job of managers is to foster cooperative relationships with stakeholders by balancing their interests (Freeman et al., 2010). And whereas traditional economic theorizing assumes that humans behave as Homo economicus, rationally pursuing their self-interest by responding to financial incentives, stakeholder theory holds that human behavior is much more complex than that (Freeman et al., 2010; Jones, 1995).

title: Given these differences, the economic turn in strategic management took the development of strategy theory in a rather different direction than the one envisage
excerpt: Given these differences, the economic turn in strategic management took the development of strategy theory in a rather different direction than the one envisaged by stakeholder theorists. At heart, stakeholder theorists see strategic management as managing social relationships: t
search_text: Given these differences, the economic turn in strategic management took the development of strategy theory in a rather different direction than the one envisaged by stakeholder theorists. At heart, stakeholder theorists see strategic management as managing social relationships: the central idea of the theory is that strategy is about building the fair and durable relationships with the firm’s stakeholders that are essential to value creation (Dmytriyev et al., 2021). In that sense, stakeholder theory is a theory that explicitly incorporates an economic dimension (value creation), a social dimension (managing relationships) and a moral dimension (fairness). This contrasts with traditional economic theorizing, which eliminates the social and moral dimensions of human interactions by reducing all interactions to arm’s length exchanges that rely on monetary incentives to align interests. By heavily leaning on traditional economic theorizing, much of the work in the strategy field in the 1980s and 1990s ended up largely ignoring the social and moral side of strategy and organization.

title: A second reason for the divergence between stakeholder theory and strategic management is that stakeholder theory became increasingly concerned with normative e
excerpt: A second reason for the divergence between stakeholder theory and strategic management is that stakeholder theory became increasingly concerned with normative ethics (Dmytriyev et al., 2021). Donaldson and Preston (1995) identified three varieties of stakeholder theory: (1) descr
search_text: A second reason for the divergence between stakeholder theory and strategic management is that stakeholder theory became increasingly concerned with normative ethics (Dmytriyev et al., 2021). Donaldson and Preston (1995) identified three varieties of stakeholder theory: (1) descriptive work that describes what managers do when managing stakeholders, (2) normative work that prescribes what managers ought to do based on moral and philosophical principles, and (3) instrumental work that explains the relationship between stakeholder management and firm performance. Of these three varieties, instrumental stakeholder theory is the natural bridge between stakeholder theory and other strategic management scholarship. However, in the 1980s and 1990s, the stakeholder literature was primarily descriptive and normative, with only limited work of the instrumental variety and almost no empirical work (Dmytriyev et al., 2021; Laplume et al., 2008). As a result, stakeholder theory seemed to many strategy scholars to be more in the domain of (applied) philosophy than management.

title: Against this background, we can interpret the more recent developments at the intersection of strategy and stakeholder theory as a rejoining of themes. Over the
excerpt: Against this background, we can interpret the more recent developments at the intersection of strategy and stakeholder theory as a rejoining of themes. Over the past 15 years we see a rapprochement between the two literatures, resulting in work that is explicitly aimed at bridgin
search_text: Against this background, we can interpret the more recent developments at the intersection of strategy and stakeholder theory as a rejoining of themes. Over the past 15 years we see a rapprochement between the two literatures, resulting in work that is explicitly aimed at bridging the gap between the (economic) theorizing in strategy and the ethical concerns of stakeholder theorists. One reason for this rapprochement is no doubt a strongly felt practical need among both scholars and practitioners to reconsider the role of business in the wake of the corporate scandals of the early 2000s, the 2007–2008 financial crisis, and the mounting societal pressure on firms to embrace their social responsibility, which has culminated in initiatives such as the UN’s 17 Sustainable Development Goals (Amis et al., 2020).1

title: Another, more theoretical reason is that in the past 20 years, both strategy and economics research have developed in ways that are well-aligned with a stakehol
excerpt: Another, more theoretical reason is that in the past 20 years, both strategy and economics research have developed in ways that are well-aligned with a stakeholder view of the firm. First, strategy scholars have largely shifted their attention from explaining competitive advantag
search_text: Another, more theoretical reason is that in the past 20 years, both strategy and economics research have developed in ways that are well-aligned with a stakeholder view of the firm. First, strategy scholars have largely shifted their attention from explaining competitive advantage, typically defined in terms of a firm’s superior ability to generate economic profit, to the complex relationship between value creation and value appropriation. This development has gone hand in hand with a shift from a unitary agent view of the firm to a nexus of contracts view (Asher et al., 2005; Coff, 1999; Wang et al., 2009), in which a firm is seen as a coalition of stakeholders (Stoelhorst, 2021). Second, economics has also changed, in particular with respect to its behavioral foundations. Behavioral economists (e.g. Fehr and Schmidt, 1999; Kahneman et al., 1986) have shown that humans are not the selfish and rational actors portrayed in traditional economic theorizing, but that they have complex social preferences and respond to moral norms as well as financial incentives, as stakeholder theorists have long emphasized. As we will argue below, these two developments not only help explain the reconvergence of strategy theory and stakeholder theory, but also hold the promise of the development of a new theory that combines the ethical concerns of stakeholder theorists with the focus on explanatory rigor of strategy scholars.

As a result of this work, however, we can also discern the emergence of entirely new streams of research on stakeholder theory.

search_text: In its original manifestation, instrumental stakeholder theory is explicitly concerned with integrating ethical concerns into economic theorizing (Jones, 1995). However, the theory is nowadays mostly associated with its central proposition: that an approach to managing stakeholders that aims for fair relationships that balance stakeholders’ interests will positively affect a firm’s performance (Donaldson and Preston, 1995; Jones, 1995).2 Following earlier work by Berman et al. (1999) and Hillman and Keim (2001), strategy scholars have provided empirical evidence for a positive relationship between a stakeholder orientation and various measures of firm performance, such as financial performance (Choi and Wang, 2009; Henisz et al., 2014), survival (Vurro et al., 2021), and innovation (Flammer and Kacperczyk, 2016).

title: Additional work has also qualified this relationship by identifying contingencies (Brulhart et al., 2019; Garcia-Castro and Francoeur, 2016; Gras and Krause, 20
excerpt: Additional work has also qualified this relationship by identifying contingencies (Brulhart et al., 2019; Garcia-Castro and Francoeur, 2016; Gras and Krause, 2020) and dimensions of firm performance for which the relationship is negative (e.g. distant search in employees’ innovat
search_text: Additional work has also qualified this relationship by identifying contingencies (Brulhart et al., 2019; Garcia-Castro and Francoeur, 2016; Gras and Krause, 2020) and dimensions of firm performance for which the relationship is negative (e.g. distant search in employees’ innovation activities, see Gambeta et al., 2019). While such empirical work typically operationalizes a stakeholder orientation as giving equal importance to all stakeholders, researchers have also started investigating the impact of investing more in some stakeholder relationships than in others (Garcia-Castro and Francoeur, 2016; Laplume et al., 2022), which is in line with stakeholder theory’s argument that balancing stakeholders’ interests does not necessarily imply treating all stakeholders equally (Phillips, 2003; Phillips et al., 2003).

excerpt: The label “behavioral stakeholder theory” (Bundy, 2019; Crilly, 2019) refers to a stream of “microfoundations” research that develops individual-level behavioral explanations for the organizational-level propositions of stakeholder theory. One example is research that builds on i
search_text: The label “behavioral stakeholder theory” (Bundy, 2019; Crilly, 2019) refers to a stream of “microfoundations” research that develops individual-level behavioral explanations for the organizational-level propositions of stakeholder theory. One example is research that builds on insights from social psychology and behavioral economics to unravel the behavioral mechanisms underlying the main proposition of instrumental stakeholder theory: that a stakeholder approach will increase firm performance (Jones, 1995).3 This work offers a nuanced understanding of stakeholders’ cooperative behaviors by going beyond the self-interest assumption underlying traditional economic theorizing and considering how fairness (Bridoux and Stoelhorst, 2014; Bridoux and Vishwanathan, 2020; Harrison and Wicks, 2013), reciprocity (Bosse et al., 2009; Bridoux and Stoelhorst, 2016; Harrison et al., 2010), and values (Bundy et al., 2018; Lange et al., 2022) may also motivate cooperation. Acknowledging that depending on the situation (e.g. the firm’s treatment of its stakeholders, or the fit between stakeholders’ values and the firm’s values) different motives may drive stakeholders’ behavior, this work offers new explanations for value creation (Bridoux and Stoelhorst, 2016; Tantalo and Priem, 2016), value distribution (Bridoux and Vishwanathan, 2020), and competitive advantage (Harrison et al., 2010; Jones et al., 2018).

title: By considering the social and moral motives underlying stakeholder behaviors, behavioral stakeholder theory also naturally connects to work that moves away from
excerpt: By considering the social and moral motives underlying stakeholder behaviors, behavioral stakeholder theory also naturally connects to work that moves away from studying dyadic firm–stakeholder relationships in isolation and that considers the impact of a focal stakeholder’s beha
search_text: By considering the social and moral motives underlying stakeholder behaviors, behavioral stakeholder theory also naturally connects to work that moves away from studying dyadic firm–stakeholder relationships in isolation and that considers the impact of a focal stakeholder’s behavior on the relationships between the firm and its other stakeholders (Qian et al., 2021) as well as on the relationships among stakeholders (Ni et al., 2014; Rowley, 1997). How the firm treats other stakeholders can not only be a signal of trustworthiness (Qian et al., 2021) but can also encourage stakeholders to treat other stakeholders well (Ni et al., 2014). This broader view is important, as other stakeholders are the source of many of the constraints that managers face when they attempt to lead their organizations toward more responsible behavior (Bridoux and Vishwanathan, 2020; Phillips et al., 2010; Werder, 2011).

excerpt: We use the label “stakeholder strategy theory” to refer to work that adopts a stakeholder perspective to redevelop existing strategy theories. An example is recent work that redevelops resource-based theory (RBT) from a stakeholder view of the firm (Barney, 2018; Stoelhorst, 2021
search_text: We use the label “stakeholder strategy theory” to refer to work that adopts a stakeholder perspective to redevelop existing strategy theories. An example is recent work that redevelops resource-based theory (RBT) from a stakeholder view of the firm (Barney, 2018; Stoelhorst, 2021). This work reflects strategy scholars stepping away from the unitary agent view of the firm, which RBT imported from neoclassical economics. This view, in which the firm is treated as if it were a single individual (or an instrument of a single shareholder) made it impossible for the original RBT to address value appropriation (Coff, 1999), which became problematic as strategy scholars turned their attention from explaining competitive advantage to the relationship between value creation and value appropriation. By redeveloping RBT from a stakeholder view of the firm, the recent work adds more precision to both RBT and stakeholder theory itself. In fact, Barney (2018) and McGahan (2021) have argued that neither RBT nor stakeholder theory are complete without the other.

title: While rethinking RBT from a stakeholder perspective stands out as a prime example of stakeholder strategy theory, strategy scholars have also taken aim at econo
excerpt: While rethinking RBT from a stakeholder perspective stands out as a prime example of stakeholder strategy theory, strategy scholars have also taken aim at economic theories proper. For instance, a team of Academy of Management Review (AMR) editors has emphasized the need to rethi
search_text: While rethinking RBT from a stakeholder perspective stands out as a prime example of stakeholder strategy theory, strategy scholars have also taken aim at economic theories proper. For instance, a team of Academy of Management Review (AMR) editors has emphasized the need to rethink traditional economic theories of the firm on the basis of a stakeholder view (Alvarez et al., 2020). One example of doing so is work that integrates a stakeholder approach with agency theory by proposing that corporations can pursue multiple objectives (Mitchell et al., 2016) and by proposing that firm performance is better served when boards consider CEOs as being driven not only by self-interest, but also by fairness and reciprocity (Bosse and Phillips, 2016).

excerpt: Closely related to stakeholder strategy theory is a fast-growing stream of research on stakeholder governance (e.g. Bridoux and Stoelhorst, 2022; Klein et al., 2012, 2019; McGahan, 2020). This literature may be seen as stakeholder theory’s proof of the pudding because it not only
search_text: Closely related to stakeholder strategy theory is a fast-growing stream of research on stakeholder governance (e.g. Bridoux and Stoelhorst, 2022; Klein et al., 2012, 2019; McGahan, 2020). This literature may be seen as stakeholder theory’s proof of the pudding because it not only addresses issues that are theoretically fundamental, but that also have tremendous practical import. In the words of another team of AMR editors, “a theory of stakeholder governance could be among the most important theoretical—and deeply practical—contributions to the field of management in the 21st century” (Amis et al., 2020: 501). This literature reflects strategy scholars stepping away from the notion that the purpose of the firm is to maximize profits and shareholder value, which informed much of the earlier theory development in the field.

title: An important part of this literature applies a property rights perspective to corporate governance (Asher et al., 2005; Klein et al., 2012, 2019; Stoelhorst & V
excerpt: An important part of this literature applies a property rights perspective to corporate governance (Asher et al., 2005; Klein et al., 2012, 2019; Stoelhorst & Vishwanathan, forthcoming). Adopting a nexus of contracts view of the firm, this literature conceptualizes the firm as a
search_text: An important part of this literature applies a property rights perspective to corporate governance (Asher et al., 2005; Klein et al., 2012, 2019; Stoelhorst & Vishwanathan, forthcoming). Adopting a nexus of contracts view of the firm, this literature conceptualizes the firm as a coalition of stakeholders voluntarily engaging in joint value creation. Governance, then, is about the allocation of property rights (control rights and claim rights) so as to maximally support joint value creation. In line with earlier work on strategic human capital (Wang and Barney, 2006; Wang et al., 2009), a central idea is that firm-specific investments are important for value creation and that to encourage such investments corporate governance should protect all stakeholders that make them from hold-up (Hoskisson et al., 2018; Klein et al., 2012), which can be achieved by giving these stakeholders control and/or claim rights (Klein et al., 2012, 2019; McGahan, 2020). Stoelhorst and Vishwanathan (forthcoming) extend this reasoning in a stakeholder theory of corporate governance in which all stakeholders that are vulnerable to opportunistic behavior by other stakeholders are given such rights.

title: In addition to this corporate governance focused work, there is also work that takes a broader view of stakeholder governance. For example, linking corporate st
excerpt: In addition to this corporate governance focused work, there is also work that takes a broader view of stakeholder governance. For example, linking corporate strategy and governance, Bettinazzi and Feldman (2021) conceptualize different types of divestitures as increasingly costl
search_text: In addition to this corporate governance focused work, there is also work that takes a broader view of stakeholder governance. For example, linking corporate strategy and governance, Bettinazzi and Feldman (2021) conceptualize different types of divestitures as increasingly costly responses to conflicts among stakeholders, thereby adding to the negotiated adaptations of firms’ governance described by Klein et al. (2019). Others have noted that stakeholder governance extends beyond the traditional domain of corporate governance (Bridoux and Stoelhorst, 2022; Gatignon and Capron, 2020). One reason for this is that some “external” stakeholders—that is, those outside of what strategy scholars usually see as the firm’s boundaries—may make firm-specific investments that are crucial for value creation (Bridoux and Stoelhorst, 2022). For example, Odziemkowska and Dorobantu (2021) study contracting between firms and local communities. Another reason is that, as Bacq and Aguilera (2022) have pointed out, the beneficiaries of responsible innovation may be parties that contributed little, if anything, to value creation. More generally, there is an emerging literature that explicitly questions the comparative efficiency of different types of organizational forms (e.g. for-profit organizations, social enterprises, cooperatives) in furthering value creation and social welfare (Cabral et al., 2019; Luo and Kaul, 2019).

excerpt: There has been a great deal of discussion about whether “stakeholder theory” is actually a theory (Parmar et al., 2010). In its current form, it is clearly not a (single) theory in the sense of a connected set of relationships among concepts with agreed-upon mechanisms and clear
search_text: There has been a great deal of discussion about whether “stakeholder theory” is actually a theory (Parmar et al., 2010). In its current form, it is clearly not a (single) theory in the sense of a connected set of relationships among concepts with agreed-upon mechanisms and clear boundary conditions (Bacharach, 1989). Recognizing this, leading proponents of stakeholder theory have described it as “a genre” (Parmar et al., 2010: 406) that includes work that may be diverse but that nevertheless has “a family resemblance” (Phillips et al., 2019: 3). What holds this genre together is the original objective of stakeholder theory, which is to develop an alternative to the traditional economic narrative of the role of firms in a capitalist system (Freeman et al., 2010; Freeman and Phillips, 2002). Seen in this light, the work of strategy scholars highlighted above adds additional members to an already broad family of stakeholder theories, which is in line with the historical development of stakeholder theory as a genre of theorizing. In contrast, the stakeholder-oriented work in strategy may be seen as a discontinuity in the development of strategy theory. We will focus our discussion of the future on the promise of this discontinuity.

excerpt: Anita McGahan (2021) recently coined the term NST for the work at the intersection of stakeholder theory and strategy that we highlighted above. In our view, this label signals two things. First, it emphasizes the long-standing concern of strategy scholars with developing theory
search_text: Anita McGahan (2021) recently coined the term NST for the work at the intersection of stakeholder theory and strategy that we highlighted above. In our view, this label signals two things. First, it emphasizes the long-standing concern of strategy scholars with developing theory that strikes a balance between explanatory rigor and managerial relevance. In fact, the economic turn in strategy in the 1980s, which we highlighted as one of the reasons that stakeholder theory and strategy theory initially developed largely in isolation from each other, can in large part be understood as an attempt to increase the rigor of strategy theory. The label NST similarly signals a concern with explanatory rigor: it refers to stakeholder research that favors building causal explanations over normative ethics.

title: But the label also signals something else, which is the prospect of not just a “new” stakeholder theory, but of a new strategy theory. As we saw above, the work
excerpt: But the label also signals something else, which is the prospect of not just a “new” stakeholder theory, but of a new strategy theory. As we saw above, the work at the intersection of stakeholder theory and strategy is stepping away from two assumptions that are (either implicitl
search_text: But the label also signals something else, which is the prospect of not just a “new” stakeholder theory, but of a new strategy theory. As we saw above, the work at the intersection of stakeholder theory and strategy is stepping away from two assumptions that are (either implicitly or explicitly) at the heart of many of the traditional theories in strategy: that the firm should be run in the interest of shareholders, and that human behavior is accurately described as purely self-interested. Rejecting these assumptions means opening the door to the development of a theory of strategic management that is at the same time more rigorous and more relevant than received theory: more rigorous because it is more realistic about human behavior, and more relevant because its increased realism also gives it the potential to inform a more humane and sustainable way of managing firms—one that does not merely see firms and their managers as passively serving the impersonal financial logic of markets, but as positive instruments to shape a better world.

title: Seen in this way, the promise of the NST project is no less than the development of a new theory of strategic management: one that at least rivals the explanato
excerpt: Seen in this way, the promise of the NST project is no less than the development of a new theory of strategic management: one that at least rivals the explanatory rigor of extant strategy theory, but that also explicitly incorporates the social and moral side of human behavior an
search_text: Seen in this way, the promise of the NST project is no less than the development of a new theory of strategic management: one that at least rivals the explanatory rigor of extant strategy theory, but that also explicitly incorporates the social and moral side of human behavior and organization. After all, the work highlighted above recognizes, first, that a firm’s resources are supplied and developed within a network of relations with stakeholders, second, that acquiring and leveraging resources is therefore first and foremost a matter of managing social relations, and third, that the (formal and informal) moral norms that govern these social relations play a central role in both a firm’s own performance and its (positive or negative) contribution to social welfare.

title: We see three theoretical building blocks in the recent literature that, together, provide a foundation for a new theory of strategy. The first is the recognitio
excerpt: We see three theoretical building blocks in the recent literature that, together, provide a foundation for a new theory of strategy. The first is the recognition that we cannot understand value creation and value appropriation without putting the interdependence among stakeholder
search_text: We see three theoretical building blocks in the recent literature that, together, provide a foundation for a new theory of strategy. The first is the recognition that we cannot understand value creation and value appropriation without putting the interdependence among stakeholders center stage. Stakeholders simultaneously cooperate to create value and compete to appropriate that value (see Brandenburger and Stuart, 1996). The second building block is the recognition that human behavior is motivated by both self-interest and moral sentiments. This is especially important because value creation by interdependent stakeholders essentially takes the form of solving collective action problems (Bridoux and Stoelhorst, 2016, 2022; Klein et al., 2019), which involve a tension between actors’ individual self-interest and the collective interest. This tension can be overcome when stakeholders do not act as Homo economicus because relationships are governed and managed to successfully appeal to their social preferences and moral sentiments (Bridoux and Stoelhorst, 2016). The third building block is to view the firm as a nexus of formal and informal contracts. It may seem counterintuitive to adopt a view of the firm that many strategy scholars will associate with agency theory and shareholder primacy (Jensen and Meckling, 1976), but the nexus of contracts view has long been a building block of stakeholder theory (Jones, 1995) and simply invites us to consider the system of relationships among free individuals forming collectives to jointly create value (see Freeman and Phillips, 2002).

title: In combination, these three building blocks hold the promise of a theory of strategic management in terms of designing, managing, and governing organizations in
excerpt: In combination, these three building blocks hold the promise of a theory of strategic management in terms of designing, managing, and governing organizations in ways that trigger stakeholders’ moral sentiments and that, in doing so, allow them to sustain cooperation in the face o
search_text: In combination, these three building blocks hold the promise of a theory of strategic management in terms of designing, managing, and governing organizations in ways that trigger stakeholders’ moral sentiments and that, in doing so, allow them to sustain cooperation in the face of the collective action problems that are inherent in joint value creation (see Bridoux and Stoelhorst, 2022). As the recent literature on stakeholder governance emphasizes, this can be done by creating, maintaining, and adapting formal contracts (allocations of property rights) and informal contracts (norms) that stakeholders perceive as fair.

title: While the building blocks for a new type of strategy theory may be emerging, much theoretically exciting and practically urgent work remains to be done, both in
excerpt: While the building blocks for a new type of strategy theory may be emerging, much theoretically exciting and practically urgent work remains to be done, both in further developing the theory itself and in empirically testing it. We offer some suggestions with respect to (instrume
search_text: While the building blocks for a new type of strategy theory may be emerging, much theoretically exciting and practically urgent work remains to be done, both in further developing the theory itself and in empirically testing it. We offer some suggestions with respect to (instrumental) stakeholder theory’s main dependent variable (organizational performance), its main independent variable (stakeholder orientation), its behavioral assumptions, and its relationship to managerial practice.

title: One area for future research concerns the dependent variable of the theory. To go beyond the (often implicit) financial market logic of much theorizing in strat
excerpt: One area for future research concerns the dependent variable of the theory. To go beyond the (often implicit) financial market logic of much theorizing in strategy, strategy and organization scholars will not only have to consider economic value created for non-shareholder stakeh
search_text: One area for future research concerns the dependent variable of the theory. To go beyond the (often implicit) financial market logic of much theorizing in strategy, strategy and organization scholars will not only have to consider economic value created for non-shareholder stakeholders (for an example, see Lieberman et al., 2017), but will also need to conceptualize non-economic value creation (Harrison and Wicks, 2013). Stakeholder theorists have already taken stabs at this problem, proposing to focus on happiness (Jones and Felps, 2013) or wellbeing (Harrison and Wicks, 2013). Others have argued against reducing non-economic value to any single objective because stakeholders hold multiple basic and nonreducible needs and values (Mitchell et al., 2016). On this latter view, organizations should not be organized around one but multiple objectives. This work on broader conceptualizations of, and measurement instruments for, organizational performance links in with discussions about the purpose of the firm. This need not reduce the theorizing to normative ethics: “purpose” can also be studied as the outcome of interactions among stakeholders that can trigger different aspects of human (moral) psychology. One question that could be investigated is in which contexts stakeholders (including a firm’s managers) are more likely to support the adoption of objectives that are not in their immediate self-interest.

title: A second area of research concerns the theory’s independent variable. There is both a need for further work on conceptualizing what, exactly, a “stakeholder ori
excerpt: A second area of research concerns the theory’s independent variable. There is both a need for further work on conceptualizing what, exactly, a “stakeholder orientation” is, and on establishing convincing measures for it. For example, to measure stakeholder orientation empirical
search_text: A second area of research concerns the theory’s independent variable. There is both a need for further work on conceptualizing what, exactly, a “stakeholder orientation” is, and on establishing convincing measures for it. For example, to measure stakeholder orientation empirical research tends to rely on corporate social responsibility (CSR) ratings, which are easily accessible to researchers but have been criticized for their low validity (Chatterji et al., 2016). Moreover, the use of these ratings goes against the argument that CSR and stakeholder management are quite different things (Phillips et al., 2003). Moreover, they reflect the assessment of outside parties based on information provided by the firm as opposed to stakeholders’ own perceptions, which drive stakeholders’ responses. It would therefore be useful to develop new measures for a firm’s stakeholder orientation (see Brulhart et al., 2019).

title: A third area concerns the behavioral assumptions underlying future theorizing. Developing a behaviorally well-founded theory requires agreement on a specific se
excerpt: A third area concerns the behavioral assumptions underlying future theorizing. Developing a behaviorally well-founded theory requires agreement on a specific set of motivational and cognitive assumptions (Foss and Hallberg, 2014), which should capture the essence of human psychol
search_text: A third area concerns the behavioral assumptions underlying future theorizing. Developing a behaviorally well-founded theory requires agreement on a specific set of motivational and cognitive assumptions (Foss and Hallberg, 2014), which should capture the essence of human psychology in collective action situations. Behavioral stakeholder theory has already suggested a list of motivational assumptions, but there is a need to also consider cognition and the interplay between cognition and motivation in shaping stakeholder interactions. For example, Crilly and Sloan (2012) show that how top managers conceptualize their firm’s relationships with society affects the number of stakeholders they pay attention to. Similarly, how stakeholders cognize about their relationship with a firm is likely to affect the degree to which they will display self-interested or cooperative behavior (Bridoux and Stoelhorst, 2016).

title: Finally, while the three previous areas of research are mainly concerned with developing more rigorous theory, the ultimate goal of strategy theories is to info
excerpt: Finally, while the three previous areas of research are mainly concerned with developing more rigorous theory, the ultimate goal of strategy theories is to inform managerial practice. The practical relevance of a new strategy theory along the lines suggested above would be to inf
search_text: Finally, while the three previous areas of research are mainly concerned with developing more rigorous theory, the ultimate goal of strategy theories is to inform managerial practice. The practical relevance of a new strategy theory along the lines suggested above would be to inform work on how specific organizational design decisions, managerial practices, and governance structures can help stakeholders achieve more cooperation in the face of the collective action problems inherent in joint value creation. It is this work, in particular, that one would expect in the field of strategic management and strategic organization. Work along these lines is all the more important in light of the many new organizational forms that continue to emerge in response to technological innovation (e.g. virtual organizations) and legal innovation (e.g. benefit corporations), which often raise entirely new questions about the nature of stakeholder relations.

title: In conclusion, we fully expect the stakeholder turn in strategy to be a lasting phenomenon. Strategic management research will likely always have a primary focu
excerpt: In conclusion, we fully expect the stakeholder turn in strategy to be a lasting phenomenon. Strategic management research will likely always have a primary focus on organizational performance, but the recent work at the intersection of stakeholder theory and strategy is preparing
search_text: In conclusion, we fully expect the stakeholder turn in strategy to be a lasting phenomenon. Strategic management research will likely always have a primary focus on organizational performance, but the recent work at the intersection of stakeholder theory and strategy is preparing the way for rigorous strategy research that is no longer exclusively concerned with financial market performance. This should help future generations of strategy and organization scholars in the important work of developing theories that can inform managerial practices that will make firms better able to serve humanity, as opposed to the other way around.

Its purpose is not to make an instrumental case for stakeholder management, but to predict the outcome of different ways of managing stakeholder relations, with an emphasis on the comparative efficiency of developing fair relationships.

search_text: Flore Bridoux is professor of stakeholder management at the Erasmus University Rotterdam, where she is Director of Doctoral Education. She received her PhD from the UCLouvain. Her research interests include how to organize firms and stakeholder–firm relationships to encourage stakeholders, and employees in particular, to cooperate with the firm and with each other. A special interest is the role of morality in explaining stakeholders’ reactions to firms’ (ir)responsible behavior. Her work has been published in outlets such as Academy of Management Review, Strategic Management Journal, Journal of Management, and Journal of Management Studies. Since 2017 she serves as a Deputy Editor for Organization & Environment. Address: Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University Rotterdam, Burgemeester Oudlaan 50, Rotterdam, PA 3062, the Netherlands. [email: bridoux@rsm.nl].

search_text: JW Stoelhorst is professor of strategy and organization at the Amsterdam Business School, University of Amsterdam, where he also coordinates the Strategy group. He received his PhD from the University of Twente. His research interests are the application of evolutionary theory and economic theory in the social sciences in general, and in the study of management and organization in particular. Special interests are competitive strategy theory, stakeholder theory, and the theory of the firm (including applications to corporate governance and organizational design), as well as the behavioral foundations of these theories. His work has been published in a variety of journals in management and economics including Academy of Management Review, Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Journal of Management Studies, and Strategic Management Journal.
